newsitem.title: INDIA: Emerging economies urged to free up oil markets.
newsitem.headline: Emerging economies urged to free up oil markets.

text.p: Oil consuming and producing wrapped up three days of talks on Sunday with calls for energy-hungry emerging economies to help themselves by dismantling barriers to energy investment and trade.
But they remained divided over how to protect the environment without hampering economic growth.

Delegates agreed to meet again next year in South Africa and to consider the formation of a world energy organisation to collect data on demand and production and possibly coordinate a more unified global energy policy.
At the fifth International Energy Conference since the 1991 Gulf War oil price scare the spotlight fell on oil-thirsty Asia.
Rising energy import bills have severely hit countries like hosts India, creating a difficult choice of whether to pass international price increases onto their consumers.
"This is a dilemma for the entire developing world," Indian Foreign Minister Inder Gujral said.
Asia is set soon to become the world's biggest energy consumer, ahead of North America.

Two of the world's biggest oil exporters, Saudi Arabia and Iran, told their customers that supplies were assured for the forseeable future -- but only if buyers could guarantee the right investment climate and free access to markets.

"Countries such as Japan, China, Korea, Malaysia, Taiwan, India, Pakistan and Thailand should note that they may enjoy security of supply from the Persian Gulf if they provide us with security of demand," Iran Oil Minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh said.
"Asia should strive to eliminate trade barriers with the Persian Gulf."
Western consumers told their Asian counterparts they could only ensure supply security by opening markets to free competition and allowing more foreign investment in their energy sectors.

"As regards security of supply Asia can do a lot to help itself," said Britain's junior trade minister Lord Fraser. "Those countries which retain state controls can give more freedom to the developing and strengthening of the market mechanism."
While cheap new methods of extracting crude ensure world reserves won't run dry any time soon, concerns remain over the huge finances needed to bring new oil and gas fields onstream.
"Serious difficulties in financing developments are possible in view of the sums required," said French Department of Energy Undersecretary Claude Mandil.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) has estimated the cost of meeting the expected rise in world oil and gas demand by 2010 at $1.7 trillion, or $120 billion a year.
Oil producers also took swipe at high taxes levied on petroleum products by industrialised consumers, warning against stifling investment for bringing onstream future supplies.
"Taxation on oil and oil products...by consuming governments are not conducive to the availability of oil supplies to meet future demand," said Qatari oil minister Abdullah al-Attiyah.
Ministers paid lipservice to the ideals of price stability and the need to keep the earth clean but left none the wiser on how to close the gap in opinion.
While consumers want stable, lower prices, producers are happy with crude, at $24.50 for benchmark Brent, near six-year highs.
"All producing countries would like prices to stay high and all consuming countries would like prices to drop," said Indian Oil Corp chairman R.K. Narang.
Norway's new Energy Minister Grete Faremo called for future talks to focus on how to combat global warming.
Concern over environmental damage from a rapid rise in fossil fuel use left OPEC producers and developing nations unmoved.

"Developing countries should not bear the excesses of the old polluting industrial order by curtailing their growth potential and energy demand," said Saudi Arabia's Deputy Minister of Petroleum Affairs Abdul Aziz bin Salman al Saud.
